newsitem.title: USA: E. coli cases mount, U.S. seeks greater safety.
newsitem.headline: E. coli cases mount, U.S. seeks greater safety.

text.p: Cases of bacterial poisoning believed linked to apple juice mounted on Friday and a federal agency said it was talking to the juice industry about how to lower the risk of such incidents in future.

Health officials in Washington state, Colorado, California and Canada reported about 30 cases of a potentially lethal strain of E. coli bacteria that may be linked to unpasteurized apple juice made by the trendy California company Odwalla Inc. Other suspected cases are under investigation.
Odwalla has recalled 16 of its products and they were removed from store shelves in its distribution region, which covers seven Western states and British Columbia.
"Right now our primary care and concern is for the health and safety of our customers," Greg Steltenpohl, chairman and co-founder of the 16-year-old company, said.
Federal and California agencies investigating the cause of the E. coli outbreak inspected Odwalla's California plant, but had not yet found the source of the bacteria.

"It could have occurred any place along the production line from an apple exposed to manure to some contamination along the production line. It's too soon to speculate," Scott Lewis, spokesman for the California Department of Health Services, said.

The E. coli microbe normally lives in cattle but can be transmitted to humans through manure or improper slaughtering and can cause brain damage or death, especially in young children. More commonly, the symptoms are severe stomach pain and sometimes bloody diarrhea.
Odwalla prides itself on the freshness of its juices, which contain no preservatives and are not pasteurized. The perishable juices must be processed, distributed and sold within two weeks.
Colorado's Department of Public Health said that, in addition to four confirmed E. coli cases linked to apple juice reported earlier, it was investigating another 11 possible cases.

Two new E. coli poisoning cases were reported in the Seattle area, a 22-year-old woman and an 8-year-old girl who both became sick after drinking Odwalla juice, Seattle-King County health officials said.

Thirteen other cases had previously been reported in Washington state since last week and all but one had drunk Odwalla drinks, they said. One of those affected, a child from Chicago, drank the juice while visiting Washington state and became ill after returning home.
California health officials said there were seven confirmed E. coli cases in the state. All had been exposed to apple juice although the brand was not confirmed, they said.

In Canada, the British Columbia Centre for Disease Control said 11 people were reported to have fallen ill during October from the strain of E. coli bacteria involved in the juice poisoning. Epidemiologists had determined that four of those cases -- all small children -- were linked to the juice and two were not. They planned to question the remaining five patients to see if they drank Odwalla juice.
In the wake of the outbreak, questions were raised in the media about the safety of unpasteurized fruit juices and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) said it was concerned.

"This is the first big producer shipping to many states where this sort of problem has come up. It does give us concern and we are discussing with the industry how to approach the problem," FDA spokesman Arthur Whitmore said.
Whitmore said the FDA had asked for the industry's ideas on how to reduce the risk of a similar incident in the future.

The discussions could lead to new guidelines for handling fresh juice but it was too soon to say whether the FDA could order juice producers to pasteurize their product, he said. Pasteurization involves heating a liquid to kill bacteria.
Odwalla stock, which plunged by about one-third on Thursday, steadied on Friday, rising $0.875 to close at $13 on Nasdaq.
